Eq. ([33](#A1.E33 "Equation 33 ‣ Lemma A.1. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
with respect to $`\theta`$:

|     |                                                           |                                                                                                                       |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\bm{Y}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\bm{y}_{1}-\bm{Y}_{t}\cos\theta_{t}}{\sin\theta_{t}}.`$ |     | (39) |

Using the result of
Eq. ([39](#A1.E39 "Equation 39 ‣ Proof. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")),
we can see that $`\bm{w}_{t}`$ is a constant vector independent of
$`t`$:

|     |                                                           |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta_{t}}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}\bm{Y}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}-\frac{\mathrm{d}\cos\theta_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\bm{y}_{1}\right)\sin\theta_{t}-\left(\bm{Y}_{t}-\cos\theta_{t}\bm{y}_{1}\right)\frac{\mathrm{d}\sin\theta_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right]`$ |     | (40) |
|     |                                                           | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta_{t}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Big[-(\bm{y}_{1}-\bm{Y}_{t}\cos\theta_{t})+\sin^{2}{\theta_{t}}\bm{y}_{1}-\cos\theta_{t}\bm{Y}_{t}+\cos^{2}\theta_{t}\bm{y}_{1}\Big]=0.`$                                                     |     | (41) |

Therefore we get the closed form solution for $`\bm{Y}_{t}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bm{Y}_{t}=\cos\theta_{t}\bm{y}_{1}+\sin\theta_{t}\frac{\bm{y}_{0}-\cos\theta_{0}\bm{y}_{1}}{\sin\theta_{0}}=\frac{\sin(\theta_{0}-\theta_{t})}{\sin\theta_{0}}\bm{y}_{1}+\frac{\sin\theta_{t}}{\sin\theta_{0}}\bm{y}_{0},`$ |     | (42) |

where $`\theta_{t}=\kappa_{t}\theta_{0}`$ from
Eq. ([38](#A1.E38 "Equation 38 ‣ Proof. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).
Note that the solution
Eq. ([34](#A1.E34 "Equation 34 ‣ Lemma A.1. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
is well-defined in the sense that $`\sin\theta_{0}>0`$ always holds.
This is because $`\|\langle\bm{Y}_{t},\bm{y}_{1}\rangle\|\leq 1`$ as
$`\bm{Y}_{t}`$ and $`\bm{y}_{1}`$ are on $`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$. Finally,
using the definition of $`\theta_{t}`$, we can show the following:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\exp^{-1}_{\bm{Y}_{T}}(\bm{Y}_{t})=\theta_{t}\frac{\bm{Y}_{t}-\bm{Y}_{T}\cos\theta_{t}}{\sin\theta_{t}}=\kappa_{t}\theta_{0}\bm{w}_{t}=\kappa_{t}\theta_{0}\bm{w}_{0}=\kappa_{t}\exp^{-1}_{\bm{Y}_{T}}(\bm{Y}_{0}),`$ |     | (43) |

which gives the spherical linear interpolation defined in
Eq. ([35](#A1.E35 "Equation 35 ‣ Lemma A.1. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).
∎

Our key observation is that the transition distribution
$`q_{t}(x_{t}|x)`$ of a discrete diffusion process
(Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2.1 Discrete diffusion models ‣ 2 Background ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")))
is a categorical. Therefore, modeling $`q_{t}`$ is equivalent to
modeling the continuous flow on the statistical manifold
$`\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})`$. Here, we show that discrete diffusion
models over $`\mathcal{X}`$ can be modeled by a continuous flow on
$`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}_{+}`$. Specifically, we derive that the transition
distribution of discrete diffusion processes can be modeled by the
continuous flow on the hypersphere.

#### Masked Diffusion Model

We first show that discrete masked diffusion models correspond to a
continuous flow on the statistical manifold starting from an absorbing
state.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Proof.

Using
Lemma [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma A.1. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")
with
$`\theta_{0}=\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bm{e}_{m},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle=\pi/2`$,
we have the representation of $`\bm{Y}_{t}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                       |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bm{Y}_{t}=\sin(\theta_{0}-\theta_{t})\bm{e}_{m}+\sin\theta_{t}\bm{e}_{k}=\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}}\bm{e}_{m}+\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}\bm{e}_{k},`$ |     | (46) |

since $`\theta_{t}=\sin^{-1}\!(\sqrt{\alpha_{t}})`$. Therefore,
$`\bm{Z}_{t}`$ has the following closed form:

|     |                                                                                |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bm{Z}_{t}=({1-\alpha_{t}})\bm{e}_{m}+{\alpha_{t}}\bm{e}_{k},`$ |     | (47) |

which defines a flow that interpolates $`\bm{e}_{k}`$ and $`\bm{e}_{m}`$
on the probability simplex $`\Delta^{d-1}`$. ∎

Note that $`\bm{Z}_{t}`$ is a random variable on $`\Delta^{d-1}`$
representing the categorical distribution
$`\text{Cat}(\alpha_{t}\bm{e}_{x_{0}}+(1-\alpha_{t})\bm{e}_{m})`$. This
corresponds to the transition distribution $`q(x_{t}|x_{0})`$ of a
discrete masked diffusion model, where the transition matrix for the
diffusion process is given as follows:

|     |                                                                         |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle Q^{absorb}_{t}=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{t}&0&\cdots&0&0\\ |

0&\alpha*{t}&\cdots&0&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&0&\cdots&\alpha*{t}&0\\
1-\alpha*{t}&1-\alpha*{t}&\cdots&1-\alpha\_{t}&0\end{bmatrix}`$ | | (48) |

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Uniform Diffusion Model

We also show that discrete uniform diffusion models correspond to a
continuous flow on the statistical manifold that starts from the
barycenter of the simplex.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Proof.

Using
Lemma [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma A.1. ‣ Continuous Flow on Hypersphere ‣ A.2 Connection Between Discrete Diffusion Models and Continuous Flow ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")
with $`\theta_{0}=\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}(1/\sqrt{d})`$, we have
the following representation of $`\bm{Y}_{t}`$:

|     |                             |                                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bm{Y}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sin(\theta_{0}-\theta_{t})}{\sin\theta_{0}}\sum^{d}_{i=1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\bm{e}_{i}+\frac{\sin\theta_{t}}{\sin\theta_{0}}\bm{e}_{k}`$                                            |     | (52) |
|     |                             | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{i\neq k}\frac{\sin(\theta_{0}-\theta_{t})}{\sqrt{d-1}}\bm{e}_{i}+\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}\sin\theta_{t}}{\sqrt{d-1}}+\frac{\sin(\theta_{0}-\theta_{t})}{\sqrt{d-1}}\right)\bm{e}_{k}.`$ |     | (53) |

Due to the definition of $`\kappa_{t}`$, $`\bm{Z}_{t}`$ has the
following closed form:

|     |                                                                                                                   |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bm{Z}_{t}=\sum_{i\neq k}\frac{1-\alpha_{t}}{d}\bm{e}_{i}+\frac{1+(d-1)\alpha_{t}}{d}\bm{e}_{k},`$ |     | (54) |

which defines a flow that interpolates $`\bm{e}_{k}`$ and
$`\sum^{d}_{i=1}\bm{e}_{i}/\sqrt{d}`$, i.e., the barycenter of the
probability simplex $`\Delta^{d-1}`$. ∎

Note that $`\bm{Z}_{t}`$ is a random variable on $`\Delta^{d-1}`$
representing the categorical distribution:

|     |                                                                                                                                   |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\text{Cat}\left(\sum_{i\neq x_{0}}\frac{1-\alpha_{t}}{d}\bm{e}_{i}+\frac{1-(d-1)\alpha}{d}\bm{e}_{x_{0}}\right),`$ |     | (55) |

which corresponds to the transition distribution $`q(x_{t}|x_{0})`$ of a
discrete uniform diffusion model. The transition matrix for the uniform
diffusion process is given as follows:

|     |                                                          |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle Q^{unif}=\begin{bmatrix}1-N&1&\cdots&1\\ |

       1&1-N&\cdots&1\\
       \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
       1&1&\cdots&1-N\end{bmatrix}`$                             |     | (56) |

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.3 Generative Process on Hypersphere

On a general manifold $`\mathcal{M}`$ that is complete, orientable,
connected, and boundaryless, the logarithm bridge
process \[[33](#bib.bib33)\] from $`\bm{x}_{0}\in\mathcal{M}`$ to
$`\bm{x}_{1}\in\mathcal{M}`$ is defined as follows:

|     |                                             |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\gamma_{t}\exp^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}_{\bar{\bm{X}_{t}}}(\bm{x}_{1})\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{\mathcal{M}}_{t},\;\;\bar{\bm{X}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0}\;;\;\;\gamma_{t}\coloneqq\frac{\sigma^{2}_{t}}{\int^{T}_{t}\sigma^{2}_{s}\mathrm{d}s}`$ |     | (57) |

where $`\exp^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}_{x}(\cdot)`$ denotes the
logarithm map on $`\mathcal{M}`$ at point $`x`$ and
$`\mathbf{B}^{\mathcal{M}}_{t}`$ is the Brownian motion defined on
$`\mathcal{M}`$. In the case of $`\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$, we can
derive the logarithm bridge process from $`\bm{x}_{0}`$ to
$`\bm{e}_{k}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |     |      |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}=\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle(\bm{e}_{k}-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t})}{\sqrt{1-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle^{2}}}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t},\;\bar{\bm{X}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0},`$ |     | (58) |

where we used the logarithm map of
Eq. ([28](#A1.E28 "Equation 28 ‣ Hypersphere ‣ A.1 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
and $`\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t}`$ is a Brownian motion defined on
$`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$. It is worth noting that
Eq. ([58](#A1.E58 "Equation 58 ‣ A.3 Generative Process on Hypersphere ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
is derived from applying the time change \[[64](#bib.bib64)\] to a
simple bridge process:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}=\frac{1}{T-t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle(\bm{e}_{k}-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t})}{\sqrt{1-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle^{2}}}\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t}\;,\;\bar{\bm{X}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0}.`$ |     | (59) |

Note that the drift of the logarithm bridge process can be rewritten
using the geodesic distance $`d_{g}(\cdot,\cdot)`$ as follows:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}=\Big[\gamma_{t}\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle\nabla_{\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}}d_{g}(\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{e}_{k})\Big]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t},\;\bar{\bm{X}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0}.`$ |     | (60) |

The direction of the drift corresponds to the direction that minimizes
the distance between the current state $`\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}`$ and the
endpoint $`\bm{e}_{k}`$. Since $`\gamma_{t}\rightarrow\infty`$ as
$`t\rightarrow T`$, the bridge process converges to the endpoint
$`\bm{e}_{k}`$. The convergence behavior can be analyzed by examining
the radial process $`r^{k}_{t}\coloneqq d_{g}(\bm{e}_{k},\bm{X}_{t})`$,
which we describe below.

#### Radial Process

Let $`r^{\bm{w}}_{t}\coloneqq d_{g}(\bm{w},\bm{X}_{t})`$ for arbitrary
point $`\bm{w}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$. Then the bridge process of
Eq. ([58](#A1.E58 "Equation 58 ‣ A.3 Generative Process on Hypersphere ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
can be rewritten as follows:

|     |                                             |                                                                                                                                                                                      |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\gamma_{t}\frac{r^{k}_{t}(\bm{e}_{k}-\cos r^{k}_{t}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t})}{\sin r^{k}_{t}}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t},\;\;\bm{X}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0},`$ |     | (61) |

where $`r^{k}_{t}\coloneqq r^{\bm{e}_{k}}_{t}`$. Then the SDE of
$`r^{\bm{w}}_{t}`$ can be derived using the Itô’s formula as follows:

|     |                                           |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}r^{\bm{w}}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left[\left\langle\nabla r^{\bm{w}}_{t},\gamma_{t}\frac{r^{k}_{t}(\bm{e}_{k}-\cos r^{k}_{t}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t})}{\sin r^{k}_{t}}\right\rangle+\frac{\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}\Delta r^{\bm{w}}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\Big\langle\nabla r^{\bm{w}}_{t},\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t}\Big\rangle,`$ |     | (62) |

where $`\nabla`$ and $`\Delta`$ denote the Riemannian gradient and the
Laplace-Beltrami operator on $`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$, respectively. From
the identities in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Preliminaries ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")
and the fact that
$`\langle\nabla r^{\bm{w}}_{t},\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t}\rangle`$ is
a 1-dimensional Brownian motion (\[[32](#bib.bib32)\] Example 3.3.3), we
get the following result:

|                                                                                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |     |      |     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- | --- |
|                                                                                                      | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathrm{d}r^{\bm{w}}_{t}&=\left[-\gamma_{t}\;r^{k}_{t}\frac{\langle\bm{e}_{k},\bm{w}\rangle-\cos r^{k}_{t}\cos r^{\bm{w}}_{t}}{\sin r^{k}_{t}\sin r^{\bm{w}}_{t}}+\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}\cot(r^{\bm{w}}_{t})\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma*{t}\mathrm{d}W*{t},\\[5.0pt] |
| r^{\bm{w}}_{0}&\coloneqq\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bm{x}_{0},\bm{w}\rangle,\end{split}`$ |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |     | (63) |

where $`W_{t}`$ denotes a 1-dimensional Brownian motion. For
$`\bm{w}=\bm{e}_{l}`$, we obtain a simplified formulation:

|                                                                  |     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |     |      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|                                                                  |     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}r^{l}_{t}=\left[-\gamma_{t}C(r^{k}_{t},r^{l}_{t})r^{k}_{t}+\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}\cot(r^{l}_{t})\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}W_{t},\;\;r^{l}_{0}=\frac{\pi}{2}\delta_{k,l}`$ |     | (64) |
|                                                                  |     | $`\displaystyle C(r^{k}_{t},r^{l}_{t})=\begin{cases}\phantom{0}1&\text{ if }k=l\\                                                                                                                                      |
| -\cot(r^{k}_{t})\cot(r^{l}_{t})&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}.`$ |     | (65)                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

### A.4 Diffusion Mixture Representation

We provide the statement of the diffusion mixture representation from
[Jo and Hwang \[33\]](#bib.bib33), which extends [Peluchetti
\[45\]](#bib.bib45) to Riemannian manifolds. We refer the readers to [Jo
and Hwang \[33\]](#bib.bib33) for a detailed derivation of the diffusion
mixture representation for general Riemannian manifolds. We consider
Riemannian manifolds that are complete, orientable, connected, and
boundaryless.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

From the diffusion mixture representation, [Jo and Hwang
\[33\]](#bib.bib33) construct the generative process as a mixture of the
bridge processes on $`\mathcal{M}`$ as shown in the following
proposition.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the case of $`\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$, we derive the
generative process for the reparameterized data distribution
$`p_{data}(x)=\sum^{d}_{k=1}p_{k}\delta(x\!-\!{\bm{e}_{k}})`$, by mixing
the logarithm bridge processes on $`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$
(Eq. ([5](#S3.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Generative process on hypersphere ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.5 Mixture Paths

We derive a new family of generative processes by constructing a mixture
over the time marginals of generative processes. We first present a
proposition for mixing diffusion processes with a general time-dependent
mixing schedule.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Proof.

We show that there exists a scalar potential
$`\Phi:\mathcal{M}\times[0,T]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}`$ such that the
following SDE defines a diffusion process that yields the desired
marginal distribution:

|     |     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |     |      |
| --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bm{X}_{t}=\eta(\bm{X}_{t},t)\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(\bm{X}_{t},t)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{\mathcal{M}}_{t},`$                                                                                                                  |     | (78) |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\eta(x,t)\coloneqq\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}\eta^{i}(x,t)\frac{p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)}-\frac{\nabla\Phi(x,t)}{p_{t}(x)}-\frac{1}{2}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}a^{i}(x,t)\nabla\!\left(\frac{p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)}\right)`$ |     | (79) |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\sigma(x,t)\coloneqq\left(\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}a^{i}(x,t)\frac{p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)}\right)^{1/2},`$                                                                                                                    |     | (80) |

where $`a^{i}\!\coloneqq\!\sigma^{i}(\sigma^{i})^{\top}`$. Here, we
assume that $`\eta^{i}`$ and $`\sigma^{i}`$ are bounded and $`a^{i}`$
are uniformly elliptic.

First, define a function $`f:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}`$ that
satisfies the zero-mean condition:

|     |                          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle f(x,t)`$ | $`\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda^{i}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}p^{i}_{t}(x)\;;\;\int_{\mathcal{M}}f(x,t)\mathrm{d}\text{vol}_{x}=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda^{i}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\mathcal{M}}p^{i}_{t}(x)\mathrm{d}\text{vol}_{x}=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda^{i}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=0,`$ |     | (81) |

where we used the fact that $`\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}=1`$ for all
$`t`$. As $`\mathcal{M}`$ is closed, its Laplace–Beltrami operator is
invertible on the subspace of zero-mean functions. Therefore, the
Poisson equation $`\Delta\Phi(\cdot,t)=f(\cdot,t)`$ admits a weak
solution $`\Phi`$.

From the definition of $`p_{t}`$, we can derive the following equality:

|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |                                                                                                                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |      |      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- | ---- |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | $`\displaystyle\frac{\partial p_{t}(x)}{\partial t}`$                                                                           | $`\displaystyle=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\partial(\lambda^{i}_{t}p^{i}_{t}(x))}{\partial t}=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}\frac{\partial p^{i}_{t}(x)}{\partial t}+\sum^{n}_{i=1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda^{i}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}p^{i}_{t}(x)`$ |      | (82) |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |                                                                                                                                 | $`\displaystyle=\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}\left[-\text{div}\Big(p^{i}_{t}(x)\eta^{i}(x,t)\Big)+\frac{1}{2}\text{div}\Big(a^{i}(x,t)\nabla p^{i}_{t}(x)\Big)\right]+\Delta\Phi(x,t)`$                                                |      | (83) |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |                                                                                                                                 | $`\displaystyle=-\text{div}\left(\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}p^{i}_{t}(x)\eta^{i}(x,t)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}\text{div}\Big(a^{i}(x,t)\nabla p^{i}_{t}(x)\Big)+\text{div}(\nabla\Phi(x,t))`$                 |      | (84) |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}&=-\text{div}\left(\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}p^{i}\_{t}(x)\eta^{i}(x,t)-\nabla\Phi(x,t)\right)\\ |
| &\phantom{aaaaaaa}+\frac{1}{2}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\text{div}\left(a^{i}(x,t)\left[\nabla p_{t}(x)\frac{\lambda^{i}_{t}p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p*{t}(x)}+p*{t}(x)\lambda^{i}_{t}\nabla\left(\frac{p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p\_{t}(x)}\right)\right]\right)\end{split}`$ |                                                                                                                                 |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | (85) |

where we used the product rule for divergence in
$`\lambda^{i}_{t}p^{i}_{t}(x)=p_{t}(x)\frac{\lambda^{i}_{t}p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)}`$.

Reordering the terms in
Eq. ([85](#A1.E85 "Equation 85 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.5 Mixture Paths ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")),
we obtain the following result:

|     |                                                       |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\frac{\partial p_{t}(x)}{\partial t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\text{div}\left(p_{t}(x)\left[\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}\eta^{i}(\bm{X}_{t},t)\frac{p^{i}_{t}(\bm{X}_{t})}{p_{t}(\bm{X}_{t})}-\frac{\nabla\Phi(\bm{X}_{t},t)}{p_{t}(\bm{X}_{t})}-\frac{1}{2}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}a^{i}(\bm{X}_{t},t)\nabla\!\left(\frac{p^{i}_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)}\right)\right]\right)`$ |     |      |
|     |                                                       | $`\displaystyle\phantom{aaaaaaa}+\frac{1}{2}\text{div}\left(\left[\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}a^{i}(\bm{X}_{t},t)\frac{p^{i}_{t}(\bm{X}_{t})}{p_{t}(\bm{X}_{t})}\right]\nabla p_{t}(x)\right),`$                                                                                                                                  |     | (86) |

which corresponds to the Fokker-Planck equation for the SDE of
Eq. ([78](#A1.E78 "Equation 78 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.5 Mixture Paths ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).
Therefore, the diffusion process described by the SDE in
Eq. ([78](#A1.E78 "Equation 78 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.5 Mixture Paths ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
has a marginal distribution $`p_{t}`$ in
Eq. ([77](#A1.E77 "Equation 77 ‣ Proposition A.9. ‣ A.5 Mixture Paths ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).
∎

From
Proposition [A.9](#A1.Thmtheorem9 "Proposition A.9. ‣ A.5 Mixture Paths ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"),
we can derive a new family of generative processes by constructing a
mixture over the time marginals of generative processes
$`\{\mathbb{Q}^{i}\!:1\leq i\leq n\}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                         |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}^{mix}_{t}\coloneqq\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}\mathbb{Q}^{i}_{t}\;\;,\;\;\sum^{n}_{i=1}\lambda^{i}_{t}=1\,,\;0\leq\lambda^{i}_{t}\leq 1\,,`$ |     | (87) |

where $`\lambda^{i}_{t}`$ is the time-dependent mixing schedule assigned
to the $`i`$-the generative path.

One example is creating a mixture path by mixing the masked diffusion
and the uniform diffusion on $`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$, as defined in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Generative process on hypersphere ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.6 Likelihood Bound

We derive the point-wise likelihood bound and the upper bound on the
negative log-likelihood of our generative model, defined as the
parameterized mixture process $`\mathbb{Q}^{\theta}`$ with the drift
$`\eta_{\theta}`$ in
Eq. ([11](#S3.E11 "Equation 11 ‣ Model parameterization ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).

Let $`\mathbb{Q}^{k}`$ be a bridge process with starting point
$`\bm{x}_{0}`$ and endpoint $`\bm{e}_{k}`$. From the KL divergence
between $`\mathbb{Q}^{\theta}`$ and $`\mathbb{Q}^{k}`$, we can derive a
point-wise upper bound on the negative log-likelihood using the Girsanov
theorem on compact manifolds ([De Bortoli et al. \[16\]](#bib.bib16),
Corollary H.3):

|     |                                                    |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |     |      |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle-\log\hat{p}_{\theta}(\bm{e}_{k})`$ | $`\displaystyle=D_{KL}(\delta(\bm{e}_{k})\|\hat{p}_{\theta}(\bm{e}_{k}))=D_{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{k}_{T}\|\mathbb{Q}^{\theta}_{T})`$                                                                                                                           |     | (89) |
|     |                                                    | $`\displaystyle\leq D_{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{k}\|\mathbb{Q}^{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{X}\sim\mathbb{Q}^{k}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\int^{T}_{0}\bigg\|\sigma_{t}^{-1}\big(\eta_{\theta}(\bm{X}_{t},t)-\eta^{k}(\bm{X}_{t},t)\big)\bigg\|^{2}_{2}\mathrm{d}t\right],`$ |     | (90) |

where the inequality comes from the data-processing inequality. The
point-wise likelihood bound leads to the upper bound on the negative
likelihood of our model:

|                                                                                                                                                                                               |                                                                                                                                                     |      |     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- | --- |
|                                                                                                                                                                                               | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}\sim p_{data}}\big[-\log\hat{p}_{\theta}(\bm{z})\big]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{e}_{k}\sim p\_{data}\\ |
| \bm{X}\sim\mathbb{Q}^{k}\end{subarray}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\int^{T}_{0}\bigg\|\sigma_{t}^{-1}\left(\eta_{\theta}(\bm{X}_{t},t)-\eta^{k}(\bm{X}_{t},t)\right)\bigg\|^{2}_{2}\mathrm{d}t\right].`$ |                                                                                                                                                     | (91) |

### A.7 Training Objective

We show that minimizing the cross-entropy-based loss defined in
Eq. ([15](#S3.E15 "Equation 15 ‣ Objective ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
guarantees maximizing the likelihood of our generative model defined as
the parameterized mixture process in
Eq. ([11](#S3.E11 "Equation 11 ‣ Model parameterization ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).

We start with deriving a uniform bound for the drift of the bridge
process defined in
Eq. ([5](#S3.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Generative process on hypersphere ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")):

|     |                                                |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |     |      |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\Big\|\eta^{l}(z,t)\Big\|_{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left\|\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle z,\bm{e}_{l}\rangle(\bm{e}_{l}-\langle z,\bm{e}_{l}\rangle z)}{\sqrt{1-\langle z,\bm{e}_{l}\rangle^{2}}}\right\|_{2}=\gamma_{t}\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle z,\bm{e}_{l}\rangle\leq\pi\gamma_{t}.`$ |     | (92) |

Then the triangle inequality gives the following:

|     |     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |     |      |
| --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ---- |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\left\|\sum^{d}_{l=1}\big\langle p_{\theta}(x,t),\bm{e}_{l}\big\rangle\eta^{l}(x,t)-\eta^{k}(x,t)\right\|^{2}_{2}\leq\left(\sum^{d}_{l=1}\Big\lvert\big\langle p_{\theta}(x,t),\bm{e}_{l}\big\rangle-\delta_{k,l}\Big\rvert\big\|\eta^{l}(x,t)\big\|_{2}\right)^{2}`$ |     | (93) |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\leq\pi^{2}\gamma^{2}_{t}\left(\sum^{d}_{l=1}\Big\lvert\big\langle p_{\theta}(x,t),\bm{e}_{l}\big\rangle-\delta_{k,l}\Big\rvert\right)^{2}\leq-2\pi^{2}\gamma^{2}_{t}\log\Big\langle p_{\theta}(x,t),\bm{e}_{k}\Big\rangle.`$                                         |     | (94) |

From
Eq. ([94](#A1.E94 "Equation 94 ‣ A.7 Training Objective ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")),
we derive the upper bound for the maximum likelihood training objective
$`\mathcal{L}(\theta)`$ in
Eq. ([14](#S3.E14 "Equation 14 ‣ Objective ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
as follows:

|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |                                                                                            |                                                                              |     |     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)`$                                                       | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{e}_{k}\sim p\_{data}\\    |
| \bm{X}\sim\mathbb{Q}^{k}\end{subarray}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\int^{T}_{0}\sigma_{t}^{-2}\Bigg\|\sum^{d}_{l=1}\big\langle p_{\theta}(\bm{X}_{t},t),\bm{e}_{l}\big\rangle\eta^{l}(\bm{X}_{t},t)-\eta^{k}(\bm{X}_{t},t)\Bigg\|^{2}_{2}\mathrm{d}t\right]`$ |                                                                                            | (95)                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |                                                                                            | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{e}_{k}\sim p\_{data}\\ |
| \bm{X}\sim\mathbb{Q}^{k}\end{subarray}}\left[\int^{T}_{0}-\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma^{2}_{t}}{\sigma^{2}_{t}}\log\big\langle p_{\theta}(\bm{X}_{t},t),\bm{e}_{k}\big\rangle\mathrm{d}t\right]`$                                                          |                                                                                            | (96)                                                                         |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}&\leq\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{e}_{k}\sim p\_{data}\\ |

\bm{X}\sim\mathbb{Q}^{k}\end{subarray}}\left[\left(\sup*{t\in[0,T-\epsilon]}\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma^{2}*{t}}{\sigma^{2}_{t}}\right)\int^{T-\epsilon}_{0}-\log\big\langle p*{\theta}(\bm{X}*{t},t),\bm{e}_{k}\big\rangle\mathrm{d}t\right]\\
&\quad\quad+\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{e}_{k}\sim p_{data}\\
\bm{X}\sim\mathbb{Q}^{k}\end{subarray}}\left[\int^{T}_{T-\epsilon}-\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma^{2}_{t}}{\sigma^{2}_{t}}\log\big\langle p_{\theta}(\bm{X}_{t},t),\bm{e}_{k}\big\rangle\mathrm{d}t\right]\end{split}`$ |  |  | (97) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq M\_{\epsilon}\mathcal{L}^{CE}(\theta)+F(\epsilon),`$ | | (98) |

where $`F(\epsilon)`$ denotes the last term of
Eq. ([97](#A1.E97 "Equation 97 ‣ A.7 Training Objective ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")).
Since $`\bm{X}\!\sim\!\mathbb{Q}^{k}`$ is the bridge process with
endpoint $`\bm{e}_{k}`$, $`\bm{X}_{t}`$ converges to $`\bm{e}_{k}`$ as
$`t\rightarrow T`$ and
$`\langle p_{\theta}(\bm{X}_{T-\epsilon},T-\epsilon),\bm{e}_{k}\rangle\approx 1`$
for sufficiently small $`\epsilon>0`$. As a result,
$`F(\epsilon)\approx 0`$ for sufficiently small $`\epsilon`$, which lead
to the following result:

|     |                                                                     |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)\leq M\mathcal{L}^{CE}(\theta),`$ |     | (99) |

for some constant $`M>0`$. Therefore, minimizing the cross-entropy-based
loss $`\mathcal{L}^{CE}(\theta)`$ approximately guarantees maximizing
the likelihood.

### A.8 Projected Processes

Let $`\bm{X}_{t|0,T}`$ denote the mixture process
$`\{\bm{X}_{t}\}^{T}_{t=0}`$ on $`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$ conditioned to the
endpoints $`\bm{X}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0}`$ and $`\bm{X}_{T}=\bm{x}_{1}`$. Then
$`\bm{X}_{t|0,T}`$ corresponds to a bridge process described by the
following SDE:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |     |       |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}=\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle(\bm{x}_{1}-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t})}{\sqrt{1-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle^{2}}}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t},\;\bar{\bm{X}}_{0}=\bm{x}_{0}.`$ |     | (100) |

We can derive the projection
$`z^{T}_{t}=\langle\bm{X}_{t|0,T},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle`$ using the Itô’s
formula for $`f_{T}(\cdot)\coloneqq\langle\cdot,\bm{x}_{1}\rangle`$:

|                                                                                                                        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |       |       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----- |
|                                                                                                                        | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathrm{d}z^{T}_{t}&=\left[\left\langle\nabla f_{T}(\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}),\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle(\bm{x}_{1}-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t})}{\sqrt{1-\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle^{2}}}\right\rangle\!+\!\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}_{t}\Delta f_{T}(\bar{\bm{X}}\_{t})\right]\!\mathrm{d}t\\ |
| &\phantom{==}+\sigma*{t}\Big\langle\nabla f*{T}(\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}),\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}^{d}_{t}\Big\rangle\end{split}`$ |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | (101) |
|                                                                                                                        | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}&=\left[\left\langle\bm{x}_{1}-\left\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\right\rangle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\gamma*{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!z^{T}*{t}}{\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}}\Big(\bm{x}_{1}-\left\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\right\rangle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t}\Big)\right\rangle-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{T}\_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t\\                                   |
| &\phantom{==}+\sigma*{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{T}*{t})^{2}}\mathrm{d}W\_{t}\end{split}`$                                          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | (102) |
|                                                                                                                        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | $`\displaystyle=\left[\gamma_{t}\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!z^{T}_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{T}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}\mathrm{d}W_{t},`$ |       | (103) |

where we have used the identities
$`\nabla f_{T}(\bm{z})=\bm{x}_{1}-\langle\bm{z},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle\bm{z},\Delta f_{T}(\bm{z})=-(d-1)\langle\bm{z},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle`$.
Note that the Laplace-Beltrami operator defined on $`\mathbb{S}^{d-1}`$
has a simple and tractable form due to the radial symmetry of the
hypersphere.

Similarly, $`z^{0}_{t}=\langle\bar{\bm{X}}_{t},\bm{x}_{0}\rangle`$ can
be derived using Itô’s formula for
$`f_{0}(\bm{z})\coloneqq\langle\bm{z},\bm{x}_{0}\rangle`$:

|     |                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}z^{0}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left[\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!z^{T}_{t}}{\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}}\Big(\langle\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle-z^{0}_{t}z^{T}_{t}\Big)-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{0}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{0}_{t})^{2}}\mathrm{d}W_{t}.`$ |     | (104) |

#### Masked Diffusion

Since the masked bridge process has $`\bm{x}_{0}=\bm{e}_{m}`$ and
$`\bm{x}_{1}=\bm{e}_{k}`$ with $`\langle\bm{e}_{m},\bm{e}_{k}\rangle=0`$
for all non-mask token $`\bm{e}_{k}`$, the projected processes are
described as the follows:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |       |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}z^{l}_{t}=\left[\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}z^{k}_{t}}{\sqrt{1-(z^{k}_{t})^{2}}}\bigg(\delta_{l,k}-z^{l}_{t}z^{k}_{t}\bigg)-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{l}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{l}_{t})^{2}}\mathrm{d}W^{l}_{t},`$ |     | (105) |

with initial condition $`z^{l}_{0}=0`$ for all $`l`$ and $`W^{l}_{t}`$
are 1-dimensional standard Wiener processes.

#### Uniform Diffusion

The uniform bridge process has
$`\bm{x}_{0}=\sum^{d}_{i=1}\bm{e}_{i}/\sqrt{d}`$ and
$`\bm{x}_{1}=\bm{e}_{k}`$, and the projected processes have a simple
form:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}&\mathrm{d}z^{l}_{t}=\left[\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}z^{k}_{t}}{\sqrt{1-(z^{k}_{t})^{2}}}\bigg(A*{l,k}-z^{l}*{t}z^{k}_{t}\bigg)-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{l}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{l}_{t})^{2}}\mathrm{d}W^{l}_{t},\\[5.0pt] |

&A\_{l,k}=\begin{cases}1/\sqrt{d}&\text{ if }l\neq k\\
1&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}\end{split}`$ | | | (106) |

with initial condition $`z^{l}_{0}=1/\sqrt{d}`$ for all $`l`$.

### A.9 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry

Here we derive the parameters of the Riemannian normal distribution from
the projected processes:

|     |                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}z^{T}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left[\gamma_{t}\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!z^{T}_{t}\,\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{T}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}W^{T}_{t},`$                                              |     | (107) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{d}z^{0}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left[\gamma_{t}\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!z^{T}_{t}}{\sqrt{1-(z^{T}_{t})^{2}}}\Big(z^{T}_{0}-z^{0}_{t}z^{T}_{t}\Big)-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}_{t}}{2}z^{0}_{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\sqrt{1-(z^{0}_{t})^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}W^{0}_{t},`$ |     | (108) |

with initial conditions
$`z^{T}_{0}=\left\langle\bm{X}_{0},\bm{X}_{T}\right\rangle`$ and
$`z^{0}_{0}=1`$. From the definition
$`z^{T}_{t}\coloneqq\langle\bm{X}_{t|0,T},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle`$, we
establish the connection between the mean projection
$`\mathbb{E}z^{T}_{t}`$ and the parameters $`\alpha_{t}`$ and
$`\rho_{t}`$:

|     |                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}z^{T}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\big\langle\exp_{\bm{\mu}_{t}}(\rho_{t}\bm{z}),\bm{x}_{1}\big\rangle,\;\;\bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_{T_{\bm{\mu}_{t}}\mathbb{S}^{d}}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})`$                                                                                                                                 |     | (109) |
|     |                                      | $`\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{Eq.}~\eqref{eq:sphere_exp_log}}}{{\phantom{..}=\phantom{..}}}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\left\langle\cos(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\bm{\mu}_{t}+\sin(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\frac{\bm{z}}{\|\bm{z}\|},\bm{x}_{1}\right\rangle`$                                                                          |     | (110) |
|     |                                      | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\bigg(\cos(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\left\langle\bm{\mu}_{t},\bm{x}_{1}\right\rangle\bigg)+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\bigg(\sin(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\left\langle\frac{\bm{z}}{\|\bm{z}\|},\bm{x}_{1}\right\rangle\bigg)}_{=0}`$                                                                  |     | (111) |
|     |                                      | $`\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{Eq.}~\eqref{eq:riemannian_normal}}}{{\phantom{..}=\phantom{..}}}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\cos(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\left\langle\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\sin\phi_{0}}\bm{x}_{1}+\left(\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}^{2}}-\frac{\alpha_{t}\cos\phi_{0}}{\sin\phi_{0}}\right)\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{1}\right\rangle`$ |     | (112) |
|     |                                      | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\cos(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\left(\sin\phi_{0}\alpha_{t}+\cos\phi_{0}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}^{2}}\right),`$                                                                                                                                                                                             |     | (113) |

for
$`\phi_{0}\!\coloneqq\!\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\langle\bm{X}_{0},\!\bm{X}_{T}\rangle`$,
where the last term in
Eq. ([111](#A1.E111 "Equation 111 ‣ A.9 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ Appendix A Derivations ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))
is zero due to radial symmetry. Similarly,

|     |                                                                                                                            |                                                                                       |     |       |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}z^{0}_{t}\approx\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\langle\exp_{\bm{\mu}_{t}}(\rho_{t}\bm{z}),\bm{x}_{0}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\cos(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}^{2}},`$ |     | (114) |

Notably, we have the following identity for
$`\bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_{T_{\bm{\mu}_{t}}\mathbb{S}^{d}}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |       |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{z}}\cos(\rho_{t}\|\bm{z}\|)=e^{-\rho_{t}^{2}/2}{}_{1}f_{1}\left(\frac{d}{2},\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\rho_{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\coloneqq F_{d}(\rho_{t}),`$ |     | (115) |

where $`{}_{1}f_{1}`$ denotes the Kummer function, also known as the
confluent hypergeometric function. Therefore, the parameters
$`\alpha_{t}`$ and $`\rho_{t}`$ can be derived from the mean projections
$`\mathbb{E}z^{T}_{t}`$ and $`\mathbb{E}z^{0}_{t}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                  |                                                                                                             |     |       |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\alpha_{t}=\sqrt{\frac{(\mathbb{E}z^{T}_{t}/\mathbb{E}z^{0}_{t}-\cos\phi_{0})^{2}}{\sin^{2}\phi_{0}+(\mathbb{E}z^{T}_{t}/\mathbb{E}z^{0}_{t}-\cos\phi_{0})^{2}}}\;,\;\;\rho_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=F_{d}^{\scalebox{0.85}[1.0]{-}1}\left(\mathbb{E}z^{0}_{t}/\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}^{2}}\right).`$ |     | (116) |

### A.10 Comparison with Prior Work

#### Comparison with Discrete Diffusion Models

Discrete diffusion models \[[2](#bib.bib2), [39](#bib.bib39),
[49](#bib.bib49), [52](#bib.bib52)\] do not fully leverage the power of
iterative refinement, which is the key to generative modeling of
continuous data, for example, image synthesis \[[48](#bib.bib48),
[19](#bib.bib19)\] and video generation \[[46](#bib.bib46),
[5](#bib.bib5)\]. In discrete diffusion models, the progressive
corruption during the forward process is modeled by stochastic jumps
between states in Markov chains. Since denoising is achieved by jumping
between states, discrete diffusion loses valuable signals during
refinement, which limits the generative performance and controllability.
In contrast, our RDLM takes a continuous approach using the geometry of
the statistical manifold and the hypersphere, and therefore avoids the
signal loss that occurs during state transitions in discrete diffusion
models, fully leveraging iterative refinement.

#### Advantage of Continuous Approach

Due to fully leveraging the iterative refinement, RDLM can generate
higher-quality samples, outperforming discrete diffusion models across
diverse domains. Furthermore, our continuous approach offers additional
advantages: (1) _Controllable generation_: Using a continuous diffusion
model enables direct application of guidance, e.g.,
classifier \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] and classifier-free
guidance \[[26](#bib.bib26)\]. (2) _Optimized design choices_: Benefit
from advancements in continuous diffusion, e.g., optimized noise
schedule \[[34](#bib.bib34), [9](#bib.bib9), [31](#bib.bib31)\] and
self-conditioning \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. (3) _Efficient sampling_: Our
framework supports efficient and scalable sampling strategies such as
DPM-Solver \[[40](#bib.bib40), [41](#bib.bib41)\]. In contrast, discrete
diffusion models are restricted to using a simple ancestral sampling
strategy.

#### Comparison with Flow Matching

Our method outperforms previous works using flow
matching \[[12](#bib.bib12), [15](#bib.bib15)\] due to three key
contributions: (1) generalization of discrete diffusion, (2)
parameterization and training objectives, and (3) scalability to higher
dimensions.

First, our method generalizes discrete diffusion models, the current
state-of-the-art in language modeling, and introduces a novel mixture
path process that enhances performance. In contrast, prior works using
flow matching \[[12](#bib.bib12), [15](#bib.bib15)\] lack a direct
connection to discrete diffusion models, resulting in a suboptimal
design that leads to inferior performance. Notably, flow matching-based
approaches are a special case of our method, as shown in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling").

Second, we introduce a novel parameterization
(Eq. ([10](#S3.E10 "Equation 10 ‣ Model parameterization ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")))
and cross-entropy-based training loss
(Eq. ([15](#S3.E15 "Equation 15 ‣ Objective ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))),
similar to the loss used in discrete diffusion models. This loss
optimizes the likelihood during training, and when combined with our
importance sampling loss
(Eq. ([16](#S3.E16 "Equation 16 ‣ Importance sampling ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling")),
achieves a superior performance. In comparison, [Cheng et al.
\[12\]](#bib.bib12) uses a simple flow matching loss that does not
guarantee maximum likelihood optimization.

Lastly, prior works are restricted to small vocabularies due to the
difficulty of learning a generative process on high-dimensional
manifolds (i.e., large vocabulary). This issue arises from the rapid
convergence problems and insufficient model capacity, as discussed in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Generation of Token Sequences ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling").
We address these challenges with dimension splitting, which
significantly improves performance and enables effective scaling to
large vocabularies.

Input: Initial point $`\bm{u}`$, vocabulary size $`d`$, number of
simulations $`N`$, number of discretization steps $`K`$, noise schedule
$`\sigma_{t}`$, time change coefficient $`\gamma_{t}`$

1:  $`t\leftarrow 0`$ and $`\delta t\leftarrow 1/K`$

2:  $`\psi_{0}\leftarrow\langle\bm{u},\bm{e}_{1}\rangle`$ $`\rhd`$
Radial symmetry

3:  $`\alpha_{0}\leftarrow 0`$ and $`\rho_{0}\leftarrow 0`$

4:  $`a\leftarrow(\psi_{0})^{N}`$ and $`b\leftarrow(1)^{N}`$ $`\rhd`$
Initialize $`N`$ independent trajectories

5:  for $`k=1`$ to $`K`$ do

6:   $`W_{a},W_{b}\sim\big(\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})\big)^{N}`$

7:   $`\sigma\leftarrow\sigma_{k/K}`$ and
$`\gamma\leftarrow\gamma_{k/K}`$

8:
  $`a\leftarrow a+\left(\gamma\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!a\,\sqrt{1-a^{2}}-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}}{2}a\right)\delta t+\sigma\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\sqrt{\delta t}W_{a}`$
$`\rhd`$
Eq. ([18](#S3.E18 "Equation 18 ‣ Parameters of Riemannian normal ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))

9:
  $`b\leftarrow b+\left(\gamma\frac{\cos^{\scalebox{0.75}[1.0]{-}1}\!a}{\sqrt{1-a^{2}}}\left(\psi_{0}-ab\right)-\frac{(d-1)\sigma^{2}}{2}b\right)\delta t+\sigma\sqrt{1-b^{2}}\sqrt{\delta t}W_{b}`$
$`\rhd`$
Eq. ([19](#S3.E19 "Equation 19 ‣ Parameters of Riemannian normal ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))

10:   $`r\leftarrow\textsc{Mean}(a)/\textsc{Mean}(b)`$ $`\rhd`$ Ratio of
mean projections

11:
  $`\alpha_{k/K}\leftarrow\sqrt{\frac{(r-\psi_{0})^{2}}{1-\psi_{0}^{2}+(r-\psi_{0})^{2}}}`$
$`\rhd`$
Eq. ([20](#S3.E20 "Equation 20 ‣ Parameters of Riemannian normal ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))

12:
  $`\rho_{k/K}\leftarrow F_{d}^{\scalebox{0.85}[1.0]{-}1}\left(b/\sqrt{1-\alpha_{k/K}^{2}}\right)`$
$`\rhd`$
Eq. ([20](#S3.E20 "Equation 20 ‣ Parameters of Riemannian normal ‣ 3.3 Simulation-Free Training with Radial Symmetry ‣ 3 Riemannian Diffusion Language Model ‣ Continuous Diffusion Model for Language Modeling"))

13:  end for

14:  Return: $`\{\alpha_{i/K},\rho_{i/K}\}^{K}_{i=0}`$
